name: Darjeeling Hills
tagline: Tea, toy trains and Kangchenjunga, done for less
meta_description: Plan the Darjeeling hills on a fair budget: Tiger Hill, the toy train, Kurseong tea, Mirik, Sandakphu, village homestays, month-by-month advice and real costs.
summary: The Darjeeling hills rise from the plains near Siliguri to 3,636 m at Sandakphu, with Darjeeling town, Kurseong and Mirik in between. Come October to December or March to May for Kangchenjunga views, the UNESCO-listed toy train and tea gardens. Stay 4–6 nights, use shared jeeps and add a village homestay.
intro: The Darjeeling hills are the ridges of north Bengal between the Nepal border and the Teesta river. Darjeeling town sits at about 2,042 m on one of them, three hours by road from Bagdogra airport or NJP station. Below it, Kurseong is the tea town and halfway stop on the toy-train line; to the west, Mirik has its lake and orange orchards; and far to the north-west, the Singalila Ridge climbs to Sandakphu, the highest point in West Bengal, with Everest on the skyline.

Most first-time visitors see the same handful of places: Tiger Hill at dawn, Batasia Loop, the Himalayan Mountaineering Institute, a tea garden and Mirik lake. They are popular for good reason, and we include them. But the hills also hold quiet villages that cost less and feel more real: Lepchajagat in its pine forest, Chatakpur inside Senchal Wildlife Sanctuary, Sittong among orange orchards, and Mungpoo, where Rabindranath Tagore spent his last hill summers.

Darjeeling can be done well on a modest budget. Shared jeeps link every town for a few hundred rupees, the walkable centre of Darjeeling saves taxi fares, and many of the best things, such as Kangchenjunga from Chowrasta, the monasteries and tea-garden walks, cost little or nothing. The money goes on peak-week hotels, reserved cars for sightseeing and toy-train joyrides. Travel in March, November or early December and you get clear views at lower rates.

The stories here run deep. These were Lepcha forests long before tea. The hill was handed to the British by the Chogyal of Sikkim in 1835, tea came in the 1840s and 1850s, and the railway in 1881. Nepali-speaking Gorkha families built and worked the gardens, Tibetans came after 1959, and Bengali families have holidayed here for generations. We point you to the places where that history still shows, from Ghum's monastery to Kurseong's tea factories.

story.title: How a forest ridge became the Darjeeling hills
paras: Before the British, these hills were Lepcha country, part of the kingdom of Sikkim. In the late eighteenth century the Gorkha armies of Nepal overran much of the area. After the Anglo-Nepalese War, the Treaty of Sugauli of 1816 and the Treaty of Titalia of 1817 handed the tract back to Sikkim, with the British as arbiters. In 1829 two officers, George Lloyd and J.W. Grant, visited the ridge and recommended it as a sanatorium for soldiers and officials from the hot plains.

On 1 February 1835 the Chogyal of Sikkim signed a Deed of Grant giving the Darjeeling hill to the East India Company. Relations soured, and in 1849 the Sikkim court detained Archibald Campbell, the superintendent, and the botanist Joseph Hooker. In response, the British annexed the hills and the Terai below in 1850. In 1865, after the Bhutan War, the Treaty of Sinchula added Kalimpong east of the Teesta, which remained part of Darjeeling district until it became a separate district in 2017.

Tea and the railway made the district. Gardens spread from the 1850s, worked largely by labourers who came from Nepal, and the Darjeeling Himalayan Railway reached the town in 1881. The Nepali-speaking majority that grew from this history has long sought a separate identity within India, and in 2012 the Gorkhaland Territorial Administration was set up to run many local affairs. When you ride the toy train or walk through a tea estate, you are moving through that history.

did_you_know: The Darjeeling Himalayan Railway was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1999.
Darjeeling tea was the first product in India to receive a Geographical Indication tag, registered in 2004–05.
Sandakphu, at 3,636 m on the Singalila Ridge, is the highest point in West Bengal and shows four of the world's five highest peaks on a clear day.
Kalimpong was part of Darjeeling district from 1866 until it was made a separate district in 2017.
Rabindranath Tagore stayed at Maitreyi Devi's house in Mungpoo on four visits between 1938 and 1940; it is now the Rabindra Bhavan museum.

highlights.title: Kangchenjunga at sunrise
highlights.text: On clear mornings from October to April, Kangchenjunga, at 8,586 m the world's third-highest peak, fills the northern sky. Watch it from Tiger Hill with the crowds, or for free from Chowrasta, Lepchajagat or Chatakpur. Mid-October to early December gives the most reliable views.

highlights.title: The toy train
highlights.text: The Darjeeling Himalayan Railway, opened in 1881 and UNESCO-listed in 1999, climbs from NJP to Darjeeling on a 2-foot gauge, with loops and zigzags. The two-hour joyride from Darjeeling to Ghum and back, past Batasia Loop, is the cheapest way to ride it.

highlights.title: Tea where it grows
highlights.text: Walk through Happy Valley below Darjeeling or the old estates around Kurseong, see plucking from March to November, and taste first, second and autumn flushes. Factory visits and tastings cost little, and buying direct from a garden or a good shop beats souvenir stalls.

highlights.title: Sandakphu and the Singalila Ridge
highlights.text: Three days on foot or a long Land Rover ride from Manebhanjan brings you to 3,636 m, with Everest, Lhotse, Makalu and Kangchenjunga in one view. Rhododendrons bloom in April; skies are clearest in October and November. A licensed guide is mandatory.

highlights.title: Village homestays
highlights.text: Trade hotel rooms for family homes: pine forest at Lepchajagat, a forest village inside Senchal Wildlife Sanctuary at Chatakpur, or orange orchards at Sittong. Rates usually include all meals and cost less than a mid-range room in Darjeeling town.

highlights.title: Monasteries, Tagore and Netaji
highlights.text: Ghum's Yiga Choeling monastery dates from 1850. Kurseong has the Netaji Subhas Chandra Bose museum at Giddapahar, his brother Sarat Chandra Bose's house, and Mungpoo has the house where Tagore stayed. These small museums cost little and tell the hills' other stories.

getting_there: Fly to Bagdogra (IXB), about 70 km from Darjeeling, or take a train to New Jalpaiguri (NJP), the main railhead for north Bengal. From either, the road to Darjeeling takes about 3–3.5 hours via Rohini road or Pankhabari and Kurseong. Shared jeeps leave NJP and Siliguri's Tenzing Norgay bus terminus from early morning to mid-afternoon at ₹250–400 a seat; a reserved car costs ₹3,500–4,500, indicative 2026. The toy train runs NJP–Darjeeling in about 7–8 hours when services operate. Mirik is about 52 km from Siliguri and Kurseong about 32 km. In the monsoon, landslides can close roads for hours, and toy-train services are often cut back. Check current status before you travel.
permits: Indian nationals need no permit for the Darjeeling hills. Foreign nationals also need no special permit for Darjeeling, Kurseong, Mirik or the villages, but must carry a passport and visa, which hotels record. For Sandakphu and Phalut, everyone pays Singalila National Park entry at Manebhanjan and must hire a licensed guide; the trail runs along the Nepal border, so carry photo ID. Senchal Wildlife Sanctuary, around Tiger Hill and Chatakpur, may charge small entry and vehicle fees. Onward travel to Sikkim needs a free Restricted Area Permit for foreigners. Check current status before you travel.

budget.summary: Darjeeling costs most in three places: hotels in the Puja, Diwali and New Year weeks, reserved cars for sightseeing, and steam toy-train joyrides. Cut the first by travelling in March, November or early December. Cut the second by using shared jeeps for transfers and walking the town, which is compact. Cut the third by choosing the diesel joyride or a short regular service. Add a village homestay with meals included, and you spend less while seeing more.

tips: Use shared jeeps for every transfer day; a seat costs a tenth of a reserved car for the same road.
Book the Tiger Hill car only after checking the evening sky; on a cloudy forecast, watch from Chowrasta for free.
Take the diesel toy-train joyride if the budget is tight; it runs the same track past Batasia Loop for less.
Stay near the Mall or Chowrasta so you can walk to most sights instead of hiring taxis.
Travel in March, mid-November or early December, when rates fall but the mountain views hold.

months.summary: January is cold and mostly clear. Mornings often show Kangchenjunga sharply, and the Tiger Hill crowds are thin after New Year week. Nights drop close to freezing in Darjeeling and well below at Sandakphu, where snow can stop the Land Rovers. Lower places such as Sittong are milder, and the orange harvest is still on. Pack proper winter clothes and you get good views at low rates.
months.tip: Carry thermals, gloves and a warm cap; most budget rooms have no heating.
months.price_note: After New Year week, many Darjeeling hotels discount 20–40% and homestays have rooms.

months.summary: February warms slowly, with clear mornings early in the month and more haze towards the end. Losar, the Tibetan new year, often falls this month, with prayers and dances at Ghum's monasteries and celebrations in Tibetan homes. It is still cold at night, and snow can fall at Sandakphu. Crowds are thin and the toy train is easy to book.
months.tip: Check the Losar date for the year; it follows the Tibetan lunar calendar and moves each year.
months.price_note: Low season: good deals on comfort-tier hotels, except around Valentine's Day weekend.

months.summary: March is one of our favourite months. The days warm up, first-flush plucking begins in the tea gardens, and rhododendrons start to bloom on the higher ridges. Views of Kangchenjunga are good in the early morning, though haze builds by midday. Sandakphu reopens to steady traffic. It is quiet before the summer rush, and hotels have rooms.
months.tip: Visit a Kurseong tea estate in the second half of March to see first-flush plucking and taste it fresh.
months.price_note: Shoulder-season rates; Holi weekend can be busy with visitors from Kolkata.

months.summary: April is rhododendron month on the Singalila Ridge, and the forests around Lepchajagat and Chatakpur are full of birdsong. Darjeeling is mild with afternoon showers. First-flush tea is at its peak. Views are hazier than in autumn but still come through on many early mornings. Crowds build towards the end of the month as school holidays begin.
months.tip: Start walks and drives early; afternoon cloud and showers become common from mid-April.
months.price_note: Rates rise in the second half of April as the summer season begins; book ahead for the last week.

months.summary: May is peak season. Families from the plains fill Darjeeling, Mirik and Kurseong to escape the heat, and the Mall is busy every evening. It is pleasant but crowded and pricier. Saga Dawa often begins late in the month. In Mungpoo, Tagore's birth anniversary in early May brings songs to Rabindra Bhavan. Mountain views are patchy.
months.tip: Book toy-train joyrides and Tiger Hill cars a day ahead; queues are long in May.
months.price_note: Peak rates; hotels charge 30–60% more than in winter and good rooms sell out.

months.summary: Early June still works for Darjeeling town, but the monsoon usually arrives in the middle of the month. Cloud hides the mountains, landslides begin on the roads, and Singalila National Park normally closes to visitors from mid-June. Saga Dawa often falls this month, with prayers at the town's monasteries. Keep plans flexible and expect fewer views.
months.tip: Keep a buffer day before your flight out of Bagdogra in case a landslide delays the drive down.
months.price_note: School-holiday rates hold in early June, then fall quickly as the rain sets in.

months.summary: July is the wettest month. Rain falls most days, mist fills the town and landslides often block roads for hours. Toy-train services can be cut back. The tea gardens are green and second-flush plucking continues, and the town is quiet and cheap. If you come, stay in Darjeeling or Kurseong, keep a flexible return and skip Sandakphu and the villages.
months.tip: Carry a good umbrella, quick-dry clothes and leech socks if you plan any garden walks.
months.price_note: Lowest rates of the year; many hotels discount 40–50%, though some smaller places close.

months.summary: August is still monsoon. Roads are slow, views are rare and the high trails are closed. Darjeeling's museums, monasteries and cafés stay open, and the town feels like a local place again. It suits travellers who like rain, books and tea at a window, and who do not mind changing plans at short notice.
months.tip: Check road status every evening before a travel day and avoid driving after dark in rain.
months.price_note: Deep off-season rates; book refundable rooms in case roads close.

months.summary: September is a transition month. Rain eases through the second half, the hills are green and the first clear mornings return. Dashain often begins in late September or October, with family gatherings and blessings across the hills. Singalila usually reopens around mid-September. Late September is a good-value window before the October rush.
months.tip: Book October and Puja-week trips by early September; rooms and vehicles sell out.
months.price_note: Rates are low until the last week, then rise sharply ahead of Durga Puja.

months.summary: October brings clear skies, dry roads and some of the best mountain views of the year, and with them the biggest crowds. Durga Puja and Diwali holidays fill Darjeeling with families from Kolkata and beyond. Dashain and Tihar are the main local festivals. Sandakphu is at its finest. Book early and avoid the main holiday weeks if you can.
months.tip: If you travel in Puja week, book Tiger Hill and the toy train in advance and walk the town instead of using taxis.
months.price_note: Peak rates in Puja and Diwali weeks, often 50–100% above November.

months.summary: November is the sweet spot. The sky is clear, the holiday crowds have gone, and rates fall. Kangchenjunga shows most mornings, Sandakphu gives its clearest views, and the orange orchards at Sittong start to ripen. Tihar sometimes falls early in the month, and the Ghum festival around the toy train often begins at the end. Nights get cold, so bring layers.
months.tip: Pack a down jacket for Sandakphu, Chatakpur and Tiger Hill dawns, when temperatures drop near freezing.
months.price_note: Good-value month; after the first week many hotels discount 20–30%.

months.summary: December is clear and cold, with sharp mountain views most mornings. The Ghum festival celebrates the toy train in early December, and Sittong's oranges are at their peak. Snow is possible at Sandakphu late in the month. Rates stay good until the Christmas and New Year week, when Darjeeling fills up again.
months.tip: Combine the Ghum festival with an orange-season night in Sittong in the first half of December.
months.price_note: Low rates in early December; prices spike from about 23 December to New Year.

faqs.q: What is the best time to visit Darjeeling
faqs.a: October to December and March to May are best. October and November give the clearest views of Kangchenjunga; December is cold but clear; March to May brings tea plucking, rhododendrons and mild days, with more haze. Avoid July and August if you want views, since rain, mist and landslides are common. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: How many days are enough for Darjeeling
faqs.a: Plan four to six nights for the hills: two or three in Darjeeling for Tiger Hill, the toy train, the HMI and a tea garden, one in Kurseong or Mirik, and one or two in a village such as Lepchajagat, Chatakpur or Sittong. Add three to four nights for Sandakphu. Two nights in Darjeeling alone feels rushed.

faqs.q: How much is a shared jeep from NJP to Darjeeling
faqs.a: A shared jeep seat from NJP or Siliguri to Darjeeling costs about ₹250–400, indicative 2026, and the ride takes 3–3.5 hours. Jeeps leave from outside NJP station and the Tenzing Norgay bus terminus in Siliguri once full, from early morning to mid-afternoon. A reserved car costs ₹3,500–4,500. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: How much does a Darjeeling trip cost
faqs.a: A careful traveller can manage about ₹2,500–3,500 per person per day, indicative 2026, sharing a budget room, eating local food and using shared jeeps. A 4-night Darjeeling and Mirik package starts around ₹12,000–15,000 per person twin sharing from NJP, and a 5-night Darjeeling and Gangtok trip around ₹13,000–17,000. Heritage hotels and tea-estate stays cost far more.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit to visit Darjeeling
faqs.a: No. Neither Indian nor foreign nationals need a permit for Darjeeling, Kurseong, Mirik or the nearby villages. Foreigners should carry a passport and visa for hotel check-in. For Sandakphu you pay Singalila National Park entry and must hire a licensed guide at Manebhanjan. Foreigners going on to Sikkim need a free Restricted Area Permit.

faqs.q: Is the Darjeeling toy train worth it
faqs.a: Yes, at least for the two-hour joyride from Darjeeling to Ghum and back, which passes Batasia Loop and stops at Ghum's railway museum. The full NJP–Darjeeling run takes 7–8 hours and suits rail lovers with time to spare. Steam joyrides cost more than diesel. Book on IRCTC ahead in busy months and check current status.

Yes. Darjeeling is generally safe, with friendly people and a busy town centre. The main risks are steep stairs, slippery roads and landslides in the monsoon, plus occasional strikes or road closures linked to local politics. Avoid driving after dark in heavy rain, keep valuables close in crowds and check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Can I see Kangchenjunga from Darjeeling in summer
faqs.a: Sometimes, but less often. From April to early June, haze and cloud hide Kangchenjunga on many days, though early mornings can still be clear. From mid-June to September, the monsoon cloud usually hides it completely. For reliable views, come from mid-October to early December, or in January and February if you can handle the cold.

faqs.q: Which is better, Darjeeling or Gangtok
faqs.a: They are different and work well together. Darjeeling has the toy train, the tea gardens, colonial history and Tiger Hill. Gangtok has monasteries, cleaner streets and access to high lakes and passes such as Tsomgo and Nathu La, which need permits. Darjeeling to Gangtok is about 98 km, 4–5 hours. Many trips do three nights in each.
